James Gunn recently hosted a screening of *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2* and shared some fascinating behind-the-scenes insights. Here’s a curated look at the most intriguing details:

- The 1980 film Flash Gordon was a major source of visual inspiration for the director while crafting the movie’s tone and aesthetic.  
- On set, Kurt Russell repeatedly called Chris Pratt’s character “Star Wars” instead of “Star-Lord”—a flub that stuck as an ongoing joke.  
- Costume designers spent a significant amount of time perfecting Ayesha’s gown. Gunn considers it one of the most striking elements in the entire film.  
- He particularly loves the comedic chemistry between Chris Pratt and Dave Bautista, calling their dynamic effortless and electric.  
- Gunn wanted to humanize Nebula, who was originally a villain in the first film. To do that, he focused on her relationship with Gamora, framing them as sisters with a painful shared history.  
- Making the film helped Pratt process the loss of his father—an experience he found emotionally grounding.  
- The young alien girl from the Kree race? That’s Grace Gunn, James Gunn’s real-life niece.  
- Rocket’s decision to build a bomb with two buttons instead of one? It was intentional—because the device had multiple purposes.  
- Gunn praised Chris Pratt’s growth as an actor, noting his performance deepened significantly in the sequel.  
- Dave Bautista’s reaction to Ego’s “decent-sized” penis had Gunn literally falling off his chair laughing.  
- The most challenging scene to shoot was Ego’s monologue about his past. The sheer amount of exposition made it tough to keep emotionally engaging.  
- During the final battle with Ego, Pratt fell from a height of 4.5 meters, hit his head, and briefly lost consciousness—a moment that shocked the crew.  
- Kraglin’s triumphant scream at the end was inspired by Christopher Lloyd’s iconic cry in One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.  
- One of Gunn’s all-time favorite scenes he’s ever directed? Yondu’s escape sequence—pure cinematic adrenaline.  
- He joked, “Has Baby Yoda ever killed people as brutally as Baby Groot did in the Escape Pod scene?”  
- Baby Groot antagonizes Drax throughout the film—but chooses him in the end, revealing he actually loves him the most.  
- Peter Quill’s emotional final speech over Yondu’s body was constantly interrupted by Michael Rooker’s snoring—since he was lying in the coffin.  
- Gunn confirmed that the scene featuring the remains of Ego’s children is packed with Easter eggs, some still undiscovered.  
- The fight between Gamora and Nebula was directly inspired by the plane sequence in the thriller North by Northwest.  
- Pom Klementieff was, in Gunn’s words, “born to play Mantis.” He can’t imagine anyone else in the role—and teases that her future arc will surprise us all.  
- When Rocket says, “Today I can only afford to lose one friend,” he’s referring to Yondu—because he knows Yondu plans to save Quill, at his own cost.

Visa, Stripe, Mastercard, BlackRock, and Coinbase are launching a new stablecoin, OUSD

The largest financial and crypto companies have announced the launch of the Open Standard (OUSD) stablecoin. The project involves Visa, Stripe, Mastercard, BlackRock, Coinbase, as well as several dozen other companies.


Partners of the project will receive all profits from the reserves of the stablecoin, deducting a small fee for Open Standard's operational expenses. This differs from most existing stablecoins where the issuer (Tether or Circle) keeps the majority of the profit for themselves.

OUSD is positioned as an open standard, in which several major players act as both issuers and beneficiaries simultaneously. This is intended to increase trust in the stablecoin among institutional investors and traditional financial companies.

- Create an alternative to USDT and USDC with a more distributed revenue model.
- Simplify the integration of stablecoins for large companies (Visa, Mastercard, Stripe).
- Attract institutional capital through the participation of BlackRock and other traditional players.
- Reduce the concentration risks present in centralized stablecoins.

Official details about the backing of OUSD (which assets will be in reserves) and the exact mechanics of profit distribution among participants have not been disclosed yet. It is expected that more detailed information will be available in the coming weeks.

The project is already being hailed as one of the most serious attempts by the traditional financial world to create its own major stablecoin.

📌 Perpetual Futures (Perps): Trading Without Expiry Dates

Main Points
⏺ Perpetual futures let you long or short crypto with leverage and no expiration
⏺ A funding rate keeps perp prices close to the spot market
⏺ This post explains how perps work and why they dominate crypto derivatives

1️⃣ Basic Idea — perps are contracts that track an asset’s price, letting you bet up or down without owning the coin
2️⃣ No Expiry — unlike traditional futures, perps don’t settle on a fixed date, so you can hold as long as your margin allows
3️⃣ Funding Rate — periodic payments flow between longs and shorts to keep perp prices aligned with spot
4️⃣ Leverage — exchanges let you control large positions with relatively small capital, amplifying both gains and losses
5️⃣ Who Uses Them — traders hedge positions, speculate on moves, or build structured strategies using perps as core tools

Final Thoughts

Perpetual futures give traders flexible exposure to crypto markets — powerful tools, but unforgiving if you don’t manage risk.

Binance has warned its European users that it will stop providing crypto services in the EU after failing to secure a MiCA license before the deadline

On June 24, the exchange withdrew its license application in Greece and announced plans to apply in another EU country. However, with MiCA rules fully taking effect on July 1, time has run out. 

In emails sent to users, Binance's European entity stated that it can no longer accept new clients and will cease providing crypto-asset services from July 1, 2026.

Users in Poland, Italy, Spain, and France have already received instructions on how to withdraw their funds. 

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao criticized the decision, saying it's "sad to see the European Union deprive its users of access to the best liquidity in the world."

For now, this looks like a major setback for Binance in Europe and another reminder that regulation is becoming one of the biggest challenges for global crypto exchanges.

📰 Trump’s ‘Strategic Triad’: Islamists With a Business Plan

In Trump’s Middle East, Turkey, Qatar, and Pakistan are selling themselves as the responsible adults in the room, the “strategic triad” that can manage the chaos better than the old Arab strongmen. On paper, they’re U.S. partners. 

On the ground, they are building an Islamist‑flavored power bloc that talks openly about “liberating Jerusalem” and treating Zionism as a civilizational disease. Not exactly classic NATO messaging.

Ankara sits at the center of this project. It trains and shapes the new Syrian army under President Ahmed al‑Sharaa. 
The command ranks include men directly tied to sectarian killings, kidnappings, extortion, and the ethnic cleansing of Kurds. 

These are the same warlords who previously ran Turkish‑backed militias. Now they wear state insignia and new division numbers.

Turkish trade props up Sharaa’s regime, Turkish officers build his security forces, and Turkish political Islam gives the ideological frame. You can call it state-building. You can also call it laundering jihadist infrastructure into “legitimate” power.

At the same time, Turkey hosts a Hamas operations hub in Istanbul, where planning, financing, and travel are coordinated under the cover of Turkish passports. 

In Lebanon, Ankara quietly seeds influence in Sunni Tripoli and among Turkmen communities, just as Trump’s circle toys with the idea of letting the “new Syria” play a role in stabilizing Lebanon. 

The alleged moderator becomes the door‑opener for movements and networks that see Israel as a temporary glitch to be removed, not a reality to be managed.

Around this core, Qatar and Pakistan add their own leverage. Doha supplies the financial reach, soft power, and media ecosystem to normalize political Islam as just another “authentic regional voice,” while still cashing in with Western partners. 

Islamabad brings arms trade, nuclear status, and a long history of living as a “frontline ally” that plays both sides of every war on terror. 

Together with Turkey’s conventional military power, this creates a coalition that can talk fluent Washington — “stability,” “partnership,” “counterterrorism” — while feeding and weaponizing Islamist actors it finds useful.

For Israel, this is a hostile axis wrapped in the language of mediation and conflict resolution, with direct lines into Syria, Lebanon, Gaza, and the Gulf, and growing influence over how Trump’s White House sees the region. 

When Trump’s envoys echo Turkish and Qatari talking points back to him as “pragmatic solutions,” the gap between Israeli security reality and American diplomatic fantasy widens. The triad offers itself as the new guardrails of the Middle East. The question is simple: guardrails for whom, and against what?
